title_en: Fanhua Engineering Co., Ltd., Southwest Company v. China Life Insurance (Group) Company — dispute over pre-sale contract of commercial housing
ruling_gist_en: Pursuant to Article 13 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China, a company may establish branch companies. A branch company does not possess the status of an enterprise legal person, and its civil liabilities shall be borne by the company. Therefore, whether a company's branch has actually been deregistered by the administrative department for industry and commerce during the alteration of the company's legal person status does not affect the company's exercise of the civil rights enjoyed by its branch and assumption of the civil obligations borne by its branch based on its status as an independent legal person.

full_text_en:
Fanhua Engineering Co., Ltd., Southwest Branch v. China Life Insurance (Group) Company — dispute over contract for pre-sale of commercial housing

Ruling Summary

Pursuant to the provisions of Article 13 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China, a company may establish branches, which do not possess the status of enterprise legal persons, and their civil liabilities shall be borne by the company. Therefore, whether a company's branch has actually been deregistered with the industrial and commercial authorities during the process of the company's legal person change does not affect the company's exercise of the civil rights enjoyed by its branch and assumption of the civil obligations owed by its branch based on its independent legal person status.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2005) Min Yi Zhong Zi No. 85

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Fanhua Engineering Co., Ltd., Southwest Branch. Address: No. 15 Minzu Road, Yuzhong District, Chongqing City.

Legal Representative: Zhang Tao, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Wang Wanji, Attorney at Beijing Xinjie Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Chen Xiaoying, Attorney at Beijing Xinjie Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): China Life Insurance (Group) Company. Address: No. 5, Bai District, Guanyingyuan, Xicheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Yang Chao, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Chen Zhigang, Attorney at Chongqing Baijun Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Sun Yu, Attorney at Chongqing Baijun Law Firm.

Regarding the dispute over a contract for pre-sale of commercial housing between appellant Fanhua Engineering Co., Ltd., Southwest Branch (hereinafter referred to as Fanhua Company) and appellee China Life Insurance (Group) Company (hereinafter referred to as China Life (Group)), the Chongqing High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2005) Yu Gao Fa Min Chu Zi No. 13 on July 29, 2005. Fanhua Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a hearing on January 18, 2006. Wang Wanji and Chen Xiaoying, agents ad litem of Fanhua Company, and Chen Zhigang, agent ad litem of China Life (Group), appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

The court of first instance found the following facts upon trial: China Life (Group) was originally named China Life Insurance Company Limited. In September 1996, it approved the establishment of China Life Insurance Company Limited, Chongqing Branch (hereinafter referred to as China Life Chongqing Branch). On May 18, 1998, Fanhua Company and China Life Chongqing Branch entered into a "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" stipulating: Fanhua Company would pre-sell to China Life Chongqing Branch 14,400 square meters of rooms on the 9th to 28th floors of Area 3 of Fanhua Building, located at Kuaizi Street, Xinhua Road, Yuzhong District, Chongqing, and 600 square meters of garage space on the negative first floor of Area 4, totaling 15,000 square meters, at a price of RMB 66,240,000. The first payment of the purchase price would be a deposit of RMB 200,000 upon signing the contract; the second payment, upon registration, would be 20% of the total purchase price (including the deposit), amounting to RMB 13,250,000; the third payment, when the project reached the ninth floor, would be 10% of the total price, amounting to RMB 6,620,000; the fourth payment, for each subsequent five-floor rise in the project, would be 10% of the total price, amounting to RMB 6,620,000. Fanhua Company would deliver the above premises, upon completion and acceptance inspection, to China Life Chongqing Branch by August 31, 1999. The contract stipulated liability for breach as follows: after the contract was signed, neither party could unilaterally modify or rescind it. If China Life Chongqing Branch breached the agreed time limit by delaying payment of the purchase price, it would pay liquidated damages to Fanhua Company, calculated cumulatively at 0.2‰ of the housing price per day; if Fanhua Company breached the agreed time limit by delaying delivery of the premises, it would pay liquidated damages to China Life Chongqing Branch, calculated cumulatively at 0.2‰ of the housing price per day. After the contract was signed, Fanhua Company and China Life Chongqing Branch registered the pre-sale contract with the Chongqing Real Estate Exchange, with registration number (98) Yu Shou (Yu Gou) No. 0953. From July 6, 1998, to January 11, 1999, China Life Chongqing Branch paid a total of RMB 58,750,000 to Fanhua Company in eight installments.

On February 12, 2003, Fanhua Company sent a "Notice of Occupancy of Commercial Housing" to China Life Insurance Company, Chongqing Branch (hereinafter referred to as China Life Chongqing Branch), stating: now, in accordance with the modification requirements of China Life Chongqing Branch and the construction drawings, the building is fully completed, all equipment installations are in place and have been commissioned. Please take occupancy from today, further refine the finishing, and pay the remaining purchase price as soon as possible, so that Fanhua Company can promptly complete the housing property certificate and land use certificate for China Life Chongqing Branch. However, Fanhua Company has not yet submitted to China Life (Group) evidence that Fanhua Building has passed the completion acceptance inspection and fire acceptance inspection and meets the standards for occupancy.

On October 28, 2003, China Life Chongqing Branch stated that it sent an "Official Letter Urging Delivery of the Office Premises Purchased by Our Company" to Fanhua Company by registered mail, but did not submit a receipt of postal delivery to the court of first instance.

At present, the subject premises have completed main structure construction but have not undergone completion acceptance inspection and are not ready for delivery.

In March 1999, China Life Insurance Company Limited changed its name to China Life Insurance Company. In April of the same year, China Life Chongqing Branch changed its name to China Life Chongqing Branch. In June 2003, China Life Insurance Company solely initiated and established China Life Insurance Company Limited. In August 2003, China Life Insurance Company changed its name again to China Life Insurance (Group) Company. On September 18, 2003, China Life Insurance Company Limited established China Life Insurance Company Limited, Chongqing Branch. In July 2004, China Life (Group) issued a document agreeing to cancel the business license of China Life Chongqing Branch and its subordinate branches, with the relevant debts and claims of the former China Life Chongqing Branch and its directly affiliated institutions to be assumed by China Life (Group).

In February 2005, while filing the lawsuit with the court of first instance, China Life (Group) applied for preservation of the Fanhua Building property. On March 11, 2005, the court of first instance rendered a civil ruling (2005) Yu Gao Fa Min Chu Zi No. 13, sealing up the property of Fanhua Building valued at RMB 66,240,000.

On February 23, 2005, China Life (Group) filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, alleging: On May 18, 1998, the company's non-legal person operating organization, China Life Chongqing Branch, negotiated and signed a "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" with Fanhua Company for the purchase of part of the premises of Fanhua Building, located at No. 15 Minzu Road, Yuzhong District, Chongqing, developed by Fanhua Company. The contract stipulated: China Life Chongqing Branch would purchase from Fanhua Company 14,400 square meters of rooms on the 9th to 28th floors of Area 3 of Fanhua Building and 600 square meters of garage in Area 4, totaling 15,000 square meters. The project completion and delivery time was August 31, 1999. China Life Chongqing Branch would pay the purchase price of RMB 66,240,000 in several installments. Given that Area 3 of Fanhua Building had 29 floors in total, before completion acceptance inspection, China Life Chongqing Branch would pay 70% of the total price, i.e., RMB 46,368,000. After the contract was signed, the parties registered the pre-sale contract, and China Life Chongqing Branch overpaid the purchase price, totaling RMB 58,750,000. However, to date, Fanhua Company has not delivered the premises that have passed completion acceptance inspection, constituting a breach of contract. After the purchase contract was signed, China Life Insurance Company Limited, upon approval, changed its name to China Life Insurance Company, and in June 2003, China Life Insurance Company further changed its name to China Life (Group), which now enjoys all rights under the purchase contract dated May 18, 1998. Therefore, it requests the court to order: 1. Fanhua Company to immediately perform its obligation to deliver the premises; 2. Fanhua Company to pay liquidated damages to China Life (Group) from the overdue date until the date of delivery (liquidated damages as of January 31, 2005, amounting to RMB 25,436,200); 3. Fanhua Company to bear the litigation costs.

Fanhua Company responded: First, China Life (Group) lacks standing. Based on the existing evidence submitted by China Life (Group), it cannot be proven that China Life Chongqing Branch changed its name to China Life (Group). China Life (Group) is not the counterparty to the purchase contract and does not enjoy the rights under the purchase contract. Second, even if China Life (Group) has standing, Fanhua Company's application to stay the proceedings is reasonable and lawful, and this case should be stayed. Third, as to the substantive issues, Fanhua Company has no objection to delivering the premises, but as for liquidated damages, China Life (Group)'s claim has exceeded the statute of limitations, and Fanhua Company does not recognize it.

The court of first instance held upon trial: As to whether China Life (Group) is a proper plaintiff. On May 18, 1998, the party that signed the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" with Fanhua Company was China Life Chongqing Branch, which was established by the former China Life Insurance Company Limited. After the former China Life Insurance Company Limited changed its name to China Life Insurance Company, the former China Life Chongqing Branch also changed its name to China Life Chongqing Branch, with no change in its affiliation. Article 13 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China provides that a branch does not have the status of an enterprise legal person, and its civil liabilities shall be borne by the company. At present, China Life Insurance Company has further changed its name to China Life (Group), and has issued a document to cancel China Life Chongqing Branch, with its related debts and claims assumed by China Life (Group). Therefore, it is proper for China Life (Group) to assert its rights against Fanhua Company as a plaintiff.

As to whether China Life (Group)'s claim for liquidated damages has exceeded the statute of limitations. First, the liquidated damages in this case arise from Fanhua Company's breach of its obligation to deliver the premises as agreed. According to the parties' agreement in the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing," if Fanhua Company delayed delivery of the premises beyond the agreed time limit, it would pay liquidated damages to China Life (Group), calculated cumulatively at 0.2‰ of the housing price per day. Analyzing the content of this agreement, liquidated damages for delayed delivery are "calculated cumulatively" based on the continuous occurrence of the breach, meaning that, from the perspective of the purchaser, claiming liquidated damages from the agreed overdue delivery date to the actual delivery date is a single contractual right established in the contract, rather than several independent rights divided by the number of days of breach, with separately calculated statutes of limitations. The purchaser can make a claim when this overall right has not been realized. If the right to claim liquidated damages in this case were divided into several independent claims and limited by separately accruing statutes of limitations, this would inevitably change the intended meaning of "cumulative calculation" agreed upon by the parties in the contract and violate the fundamental principle of party autonomy. Second, in this case, the parties only agreed on the method of calculating liquidated damages in the contract, not the time limit for payment. For a debt without a specified time limit for payment, the creditor may assert it at any time; only when the debtor expressly indicates non-performance can it be determined that the creditor "knows or should know that its rights have been infringed," and the statute of limitations can begin to run. Third, considering the actual circumstances of this case, requiring the purchaser to separately file a lawsuit or apply for arbitration on the claim for liquidated damages before delivery of the premises does not conform to the public order and good customs generally observed by the public in daily life. In summary, Fanhua Company's defense that the statute of limitations for liquidated damages claims should be calculated separately based on the time of breach is not supported by existing laws or explicit provisions of judicial interpretations, and is not adopted.

In conclusion, the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" signed by China Life (Group) and Fanhua Company complies with legal provisions and represents the true intentions of both parties, and thus should be protected by law. Fanhua Company should faithfully perform its obligations under the contract and avoid further losses caused by its breach. China Life (Group)'s claims and reasons are well-founded. Pursuant to Article 60, Paragraph 1, Article 107, and Article 114 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows: 1. Fanhua Company shall, within thirty days after this judgment becomes effective, deliver to China Life (Group) the 14,400 square meters of rooms on the 9th to 28th floors of Area 3 of Fanhua Building and the 600 square meters of garage in Area 4, which have passed acceptance inspection, in accordance with the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" signed by the parties, and handle the relevant property title transfer procedures. 2. Fanhua Company shall immediately pay China Life (Group) liquidated damages for delayed delivery as of January 31, 2005, in the amount of RMB 25,436,200, and shall pay liquidated damages for delayed delivery at a daily rate of 0.2‰ of RMB 66,240,000 from February 1, 2005, until the delivery obligation under item 1 of this judgment is performed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 430,960 and the preservation fee of RMB 331,720, totaling RMB 762,680, shall be borne by Fanhua Company.

Fanhua Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court, requesting the reversal of the first-instance judgment, the dismissal of China Life (Group)'s claims, and that China Life (Group) bear the litigation costs of this case. The main reasons were: 1. The first-instance judgment erred in finding that China Life (Group) had standing to sue. The evidence provided by China Life (Group) was insufficient to prove that it enjoyed the rights under the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing," and it had no right to bring this lawsuit. According to an industrial and commercial inquiry record issued by the Chongqing Administration for Industry and Commerce on May 18, 2005, as of that date, China Life Chongqing Branch remained a legally existing and registered legal person branch, and had not undergone procedures for cancellation, revocation, or change of subject qualification. The evidence provided by China Life (Group) could not demonstrate that China Life (Group) lawfully succeeded to the debts and claims of China Life Chongqing Branch, or that China Life (Group) lawfully enjoyed the rights of China Life Chongqing Branch under the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing." The evidence provided by China Life (Group) was contradictory and could not show which entity was ultimately responsible for the debts and claims of China Life Chongqing Branch. 2. The first-instance judgment incorrectly found that Fanhua Company was in breach and ordered it to bear liability for breach. First, based on the correspondence between Fanhua Company and China Life Chongqing Branch provided by China Life (Group), the parties had reached a new agreement on the delivery time, and Fanhua Company was not in breach. The subject premises had their main structure topped out by the end of 1998, and were completed and passed structural acceptance inspection in August 1999. Fanhua Company was already in a position to deliver the premises as agreed, but because the former legal representative of Fanhua Company was removed and refused to hand over all engineering documents, Fanhua Company could not obtain the corresponding evidence. During the first instance, Fanhua Company had filed a "Application for Investigation and Evidence Collection" with the court, but it was ignored by the court of first instance. The change in design requested by China Life (Group) was the fundamental reason why Fanhua Company failed to deliver the premises by the time stipulated in the "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing." The "Official Letter Urging Delivery of the Office Premises Purchased by Our Company" issued by China Life Chongqing Branch indicated that the parties had formed a new consensus on the delivery time, and China Life (Group) could no longer claim Fanhua Company's breach based on the original contract. Second, assuming Fanhua Company was in breach, China Life (Group)'s claim for liquidated damages had already exceeded the statute of limitations and lost the right to win the case. The "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" stipulated a clear time limit for performance, i.e., from September 1, 1999, Fanhua Company should pay liquidated damages. The liquidated damages in this case had a specified time limit for payment. For nearly six years from the agreed delivery date, China Life (Group) never urged Fanhua Company to deliver the premises, nor did it claim liquidated damages. Therefore, the claim for liquidated damages by China Life (Group) had exceeded the statute of limitations and should not be protected by law.

China Life (Group) responded in court: The first-instance judgment had clear factual findings and correct application of law, and should be affirmed. The main reasons were: 1. China Life (Group) has proper standing. 2. The "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" stipulated that Fanhua Company should deliver premises that had passed completion acceptance inspection by August 31, 1999, not merely that the main structure had been topped out. The two letters sent by China Life (Group) were intended to urge delivery of the premises, which is not the same concept as changing the delivery time; the parties never modified the delivery conditions. 3. The "Contract for Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) of Commercial Housing" did not stipulate the time limit for payment of liquidated damages, so the statute of limitations should begin to run from the date of dispute, i.e., when China Life (Group) respectively sent letters to Fanhua Company on October 28, 2003, and April 13, 2004, urging delivery of the premises and being refused.

This Court finds that the facts found in the second instance are the same as those found by the court of first instance.

This Court holds that there are two points of dispute between the parties in this case: first, the issue of China Life (Group)'s standing to sue; second, the determination of liability for breach and whether China Life (Group)'s claim for liquidated damages has exceeded the statute of limitations.

I. The issue of China Life (Group)'s standing to sue.

Upon review, the signing party of the "Commercial Housing Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) Contract" involved in this case was China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch. This company was a branch established by China Life Insurance Co., Ltd. On March 22, 1999, with the approval of the China Insurance Regulatory Commission, China Life Insurance Co., Ltd. was renamed China Life Insurance Company. Accordingly, China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch, as a branch of China Life Insurance Co., Ltd., also changed its company name to China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch on April 20 of the same year. On July 8, 2003, China Life Insurance Company was again renamed China Life Insurance (Group) Company. The above facts indicate that China Life Insurance (Group) Company and the parent company of the signing party China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch, namely China Life Insurance Co., Ltd., are merely differences in the company name before and after the change, and are in substance the same legal person. After the establishment of China Life Insurance (Group) Company through the change, although China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch did not correspondingly change its name accordingly, on July 14, 2004, China Life Insurance (Group) Company issued a "Letter Regarding the Cancellation of the Former China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch and Its Subordinate Institutions" to the Chongqing Municipal Administration for Industry and Commerce, applying to cancel China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch, and simultaneously stated that the relevant creditor's rights and debts of the former China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch and its subordinate institutions would be assumed by the company. The act of China Life Insurance (Group) Company applying to cancel China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch constitutes a change and adjustment of its branches by the company based on operational development needs. Pursuant to the provisions of Article 13 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China, a company may establish branches. A branch does not have the status of an enterprise legal person, and its civil liability shall be borne by the company. Therefore, whether a company's branch has actually been deregistered with the industry and commerce authorities during the process of legal person change does not affect the company's exercise of its civil rights and assumption of civil obligations pertaining to its branch based on its independent legal person status. China Life Insurance (Group) Company, in the capacity of the plaintiff in this case, claiming the contractual rights under the "Commercial Housing Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) Contract" against Fanhua Company is in accordance with legal provisions. The appeal by Fanhua Company arguing that as of May 18, 2005, China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch had not completed deregistration procedures and remained a lawfully existing legal person branch, and thus China Life Insurance (Group) Company did not have legal standing to file this lawsuit, is inconsistent with the facts and lacks legal basis. The first-instance judgment's finding that China Life Insurance (Group) Company was a proper plaintiff in this case, and its determination of facts and application of law were correct, and is hereby affirmed.

2. Determination of Liability for Breach of Contract and Whether China Life Insurance (Group) Company's Claim for Liquidated Damages Exceeded the Statute of Limitations.

The "Commercial Housing Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) Contract" signed by the parties to this case stipulated that Fanhua Company should deliver the completed and inspection-qualified premises to China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch by August 31, 1999. Fanhua Company appealed, arguing that based on the correspondence between Fanhua Company and China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch, the parties had reached a new agreement on the delivery time, and thus Fanhua Company had not breached the contract. Upon review, China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch sent two letters to Fanhua Company on October 28, 2003, and April 13, 2004, respectively, titled "Official Letter Urging Delivery of the Office Premises Purchased by Our Company." The postal delivery receipt for the letter dated April 13, 2004, indicated that Fanhua Company refused to accept it. The content of that letter was a reminder from China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch, based on the fact that as of the date of the letter, Fanhua Company had still not completed the project's completion acceptance, fire safety acceptance, and rectification of environmental support facilities, urging Fanhua Company to deliver the inspection-qualified premises as soon as possible in accordance with the contract to avoid further expansion of losses. There is no evidence of a clear and specific mutual agreement to change the delivery deadline in that letter, and apart from this, Fanhua Company has also not provided any other form of evidence to prove its claim that the parties had reached a consensus on changing the delivery time for the disputed premises. Therefore, Fanhua Company's above assertion is inconsistent with the facts and is not supported. Fanhua Company also raised two further claims in its appeal: first, that the disputed premises in this case were completed in August 1999 and passed structural inspection, thus meeting the conditions for delivery as agreed; and second, that China Life Insurance (Group) Company's request for design changes was the fundamental reason Fanhua Company failed to deliver the premises on time. These were put forward as defenses against liability for breach of contract. Upon investigation, from the outset of this litigation, Fanhua Company has consistently failed to provide valid evidence that the disputed premises had passed completion acceptance inspection or that China Life Insurance (Group) Company had made design changes inconsistent with the contract during the performance of the contract. In this regard, Fanhua Company claimed that its inability to adduce evidence was due to the concealment of project documents by its former legal representative. Changes in the legal representative of a company are internal personnel adjustments. During the lawful existence of a company, a change in legal representative does not constitute a legal defense affecting the company's assumption of civil liability. Therefore, this ground of appeal by Fanhua Company also cannot be established.

According to the agreement between the parties in the "Commercial Housing Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) Contract," if Fanhua Company violated the agreed deadline and delayed delivery of the premises, it should pay liquidated damages to China Life Insurance (Group) Company, calculated cumulatively at 0.2‰ of the total housing price per day. Fanhua Company appealed, arguing that China Life Insurance (Group) Company had never urged Fanhua Company to deliver the premises, and thus its claim for liquidated damages had exceeded the statute of limitations and should not be supported. Analyzing the facts found in this case, China Life Insurance (Group) Company purchased the Fanhua Building for the purpose of meeting its office space needs. Because Fanhua Company consistently failed to deliver the disputed premises, China Life Insurance (Group) Company still rents office space elsewhere to this day. Under these circumstances, Fanhua Company's appeal argument that China Life Insurance (Group) Company did not assert its rights for a long period after the delivery deadline arrived is not only inconsistent with the purpose of concluding this "Commercial Housing Pre-sale (Pre-purchase) Contract" but also defies common sense. Moreover, in its appeal request, Fanhua Company argued on the one hand that based on the mutual correspondence, the parties had reached a new change regarding the delivery deadline, while on the other hand claiming that the parties had never negotiated regarding the delivery matter and that China Life Insurance (Group) Company had never urged Fanhua Company to deliver the premises. These two appeal arguments are contradictory, and this court does not accept them. On April 14, 2004, China Life Insurance Chongqing Branch sent a letter titled "Official Letter Urging Delivery of the Office Premises Purchased by Our Company" to Fanhua Company, demanding that Fanhua Company deliver the inspection-qualified premises before the end of June 2004. Fanhua Company refused to accept this letter. At this point, it should be considered that the right holder asserted its right while the obligor refused to perform the obligation, and the right holder thereby learned that its right had been infringed. The statute of limitations should be calculated from the date this dispute arose. Therefore, Fanhua Company's appeal argument that the claim for liquidated damages in this case had exceeded the statute of limitations is inconsistent with the facts and lacks legal basis, and is not supported.

In conclusion, the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. The grounds of appeal by Fanhua Company cannot be established, and this court does not support them. Pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

Appeal dismissed; the original judgment is affirmed.

If the monetary payment obligation specified in this judgment is not performed within the prescribed period, interest on the debt during the period of delayed performance shall be paid at double the rate, in accordance with Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 430,960 shall be borne by Fanhua Engineering Co., Ltd., Southwest Company.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Feng Xiaoguang

Acting Judge: Guan Li

Acting Judge: Zhang Yingxin

May 14, 2007

Clerk: Yu Wenjun
